title: When Agents Meet Physical Data: The Other Physics of Agent Harnesses - Dmitry Petrov, DataChain
talk_summary: Dmitry Petrov argues that coding agents fail on messy physical/unstructured data unless given a data harness: typed schemas, an execution engine, checkpoints, metadata tables, and a shared knowledge base. The talk demonstrates DataChain on video analysis, but the transferable mechanisms are caching/reuse, resumability, and typed contracts for long-running agent work.

takeaways.what_they_do: The execution engine checkpoints processed files/results so a failed long job can resume and only process new or failed work instead of recomputing everything.
takeaways.evidence_quote: If you fail, you fix the bug, run it again and catch up all the result that you have already.

takeaways.what_they_do: After expensive computation they write a Markdown knowledge file with dataset description, session context, dependencies, preview, schema, stats, and source code so future agents do not recompute.
takeaways.evidence_quote: just a set of MD files

takeaways.what_they_do: Before answering, the agent checks whether reusable metadata/datasets exist to answer cheaply in a SQL-ish query; if not, it builds a general reusable metadata layer.
takeaways.evidence_quote: instead of answering the question right away, agent ask itself, do I have a proper data sets
takeaways.numbers: 24 minutes for 90 videos; 90 videos generated 100,000 records

takeaways.what_they_do: They define Pydantic input/output models so the same Python types describe data, agent outputs, and execution-engine parallelization.
takeaways.evidence_quote: The magic part here is the data model.

takeaways.technique: Test against metadata, not raw inputs
takeaways.what_they_do: They organize a metadata layer over raw data so quality questions can be answered quickly instead of running expensive scripts over raw files.
takeaways.evidence_quote: stop running all this like complicated Python scripts on top of raw data

takeaways.what_they_do: The harness lets users specify how many machines/resources a job needs, and the engine distributes work by files and schemas.
takeaways.evidence_quote: I just need to run it in 40 machines
